analysis.one_liner: Lets the FDA regulate tobacco: ingredient disclosure, advertising limits, product review, stronger warning labels.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on June 14, 2002 with 21 cosponsors from both parties and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it before the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Tobacco is the only consumer product sold for human consumption that no federal agency regulates. A 2000 Supreme Court decision held the FDA lacked authority over tobacco unless Congress granted it, and this bill was Congress's answer. It would have made the FDA the main federal regulator of cigarettes and smokeless tobacco: manufacturers would have to register, disclose ingredients and nicotine levels, hand over their internal health research, meet manufacturing standards, submit new products for review before sale, and accept new warning labels and restrictions on advertising aimed at young people. It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee and never received a committee vote or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and teenagers, who would face fewer tobacco ads and promotions; adult consumers, who would get accurate ingredient, tar, and nicotine disclosure and stronger warning labels; and the public generally, through an FDA that could set performance standards (including reducing or eliminating nicotine), order recalls, and review new products before they go on sale. State and local governments would keep their own stricter rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children, teens, and adult tobacco consumers

how_it_helps.text: Gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services, acting through the FDA, regulatory authority over tobacco products, including authority to deem products adulterated or misbranded, require annual registration, and order recalls.

Requires manufacturers to disclose all added ingredients, the nicotine content and delivery of each product, and all internal research documents on health effects — including research not previously made public.
Authorizes the Secretary to restrict the sale, access, advertising, and promotion of tobacco products to protect public health, to the full extent the First Amendment permits.
Authorizes performance standards, including reducing or eliminating nicotine yields and other harmful components, and premarket review of new tobacco products.
Revises cigarette and smokeless tobacco warning labels and requires public disclosure of tar, nicotine, and other smoke constituents.
Preserves state and local authority to impose stricter rules and requires equal treatment of all retail outlets for tobacco advertising restrictions.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers and importers, who would bear registration, disclosure, records, inspection, and good-manufacturing-practice compliance costs; the tobacco advertising and sports-sponsorship machine, which would face restrictions; and tobacco retailers, who would be subject to advertising limits applied equally across outlet types.

drawbacks.text: The bill grandfathered existing products: premarket approval applied only to products not commercially marketed as of June 1, 2002, so the major manufacturers' current brands faced no product review while new products and newer entrants faced costly applications — a structure that favors large incumbent companies.

A standard that would ban a class of products (like all cigarettes) or cut nicotine to zero could not take effect until two years after the President notified Congress, leaving the industry's core products politically protected.
Tobacco leaf and growers were expressly exempted: the bill says the FDA may not regulate tobacco leaf production or enter a farm without the grower's written consent.
Compliance with good manufacturing practice requirements was not required until three years after enactment, delaying the tightest rules.
No advertising restriction could prohibit face-to-face sales by a specific category of retail outlet, limiting how far marketing curbs could reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health payoff would have been large — tobacco causes over 400,000 deaths a year, and the bill's own findings estimate that cutting youth smoking in half would save over 3 million of today's children from premature death and roughly $110 billion in health costs. The real costs fall on manufacturers, advertisers, and retailers, and the design has genuine flaws: existing products escape review, the harshest standards face a two-year congressional delay, and growers are exempt. Still, the central trade — industry disclosure and marketing limits in exchange for federal oversight of a product that kills hundreds of thousands annually — clearly favored the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2002, referred to the Senate health committee, and sat there without a committee vote or floor action until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on June 14, 2002 with nine other senators, including Republicans John McCain, Mike DeWine, and Susan Collins.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no markup, committee vote, or floor action afterward.
Twenty-one senators cosponsored the bill — 14 Democrats and 7 Republicans.
The 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor or the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and the tobacco marketing apparatus came out ahead: the industry continued to operate without any federal regulator, with no ingredient or nicotine disclosure, no premarket review of new products, no recall authority, and no new advertising restrictions — while spending, by the bill's own findings, close to $8.24 billion a year to attract new users. Children kept facing tobacco advertising that the bill's findings said was deliberately aimed at them.

for.name: Edward Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator (D-MA), sponsor and chair of the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its public health findings on the Senate floor, then referred it to his own committee.

for.role: Cosponsors, including original introducers Mike DeWine, John McCain, and Susan Collins
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: Public health community
for.what_they_did: The bill's findings cite consensus among scientific and medical communities that tobacco is inherently dangerous and that the industry should face ongoing oversight.

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after its referral in June 2002; the bill died there.

against.name: Tobacco manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Long opposed FDA authority over tobacco products, which the Supreme Court confirmed the agency lacked in 2000 — the gap this bill would have filled.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 14 Democrats and 7 Republicans cosponsored, and three Republicans helped introduce it — and no recorded opposition vote ever occurred because the bill never reached the floor.

industries.note: The bill would impose real costs — ingredient and nicotine disclosure, registration, inspections, manufacturing standards, premarket review, and advertising restrictions — which is why the industry's interest runs against the public here. But it also grandfathered every existing product as of June 1, 2002, so the dominant companies' current brands would face no product review while new products and smaller entrants would, a structure that tends to lock in the incumbents.
The bill expressly exempts tobacco leaf, growers, warehouses, and grower cooperatives from regulation and bars FDA employees from entering farms without written consent.

industries.industry: Tobacco advertising and marketing (including sports sponsorships)
industries.note: The bill authorizes advertising and promotion restrictions and new warning requirements; the industry's roughly $8.24 billion annual marketing effort, which the bill's findings say targets young people, would have been curtailed.

Retailers would face advertising restrictions and compliance duties, but the bill requires all retail outlets to be treated equally and forbids banning face-to-face sales by a category of outlet, protecting small retailers from selective bans.
